entry.title: Llama 2: A Source Tour of Meta’s Reference LLM Inference Code

link.title: Llama 2: A Source Tour of Meta’s Reference LLM Inference Code

entry.content:
When Meta released Llama 2 in July 2023, the weights grabbed the headlines, but the small Python package that shipped alongside them — meta-llama/llama — quietly became one of the most consequential pieces of inference code in modern machine learning. The llama/ directory is barely two thousand lines across three modules, yet it defined the template that dozens of later open-source serving stacks would copy: a dataclass of hyperparameters, a decoder-only Transformer, a SentencePiece tokenizer wrapper, and an autoregressive loop with temperature and top-p sampling. If you have ever read a newer inference framework and felt a strange sense of déjà vu, this is almost certainly the source you were remembering.

This post is a source tour of that reference implementation as it stands on the main branch today. The repository is now flagged as deprecated in its own README in favor of the consolidated Llama Stack repositories, which makes it an unusually clean time capsule: nothing in it is chasing new features, so every line exists to demonstrate the Llama 2 architecture — grouped-query attention, rotary position embeddings, RMSNorm, SwiGLU — in the most direct PyTorch imaginable. There is no serving layer, no quantization, no CUDA kernels of its own. That minimalism is precisely why it rewards a close reading.

Two diagrams anchor the tour. The first shows the four-load-bearing-piece view: the model, the tokenizer, the generation facade, and the example scripts that tie them together. The second zooms in to individual symbols and the wiring between them, including the checkpoint loader and the chat formatting rules.

Overview of meta-llama/llama: llama/model.py builds the Transformer; llama/tokenizer.py wraps SentencePiece; llama/generation.py's Llama facade loads checkpoints and runs generation; example_chat_completion.py is the torchrun entry point.

Reading the overview from left to right:

Each node in the diagram corresponds to one real symbol in the repository. Follow the links to see them in place:

  • ModelArgs, L20 — a plain dataclass holding dim, n_layers, n_heads, and n_kv_heads. That last field defaults to None, and when it does, the code falls back to n_heads; setting it smaller is the entire grouped-query attention mechanism, one line of configuration instead of a new class.
  • Transformer, L413 — the top-level nn.Module. It owns a ParallelEmbedding, a ModuleList of n_layers blocks, a final RMSNorm, a ColumnParallelLinear projection to vocab_size, and a precomputed RoPE table sized to max_seq_len * 2.
  • Attention, L176 — multi-head attention built on fairscale’s ColumnParallelLinear and RowParallelLinear, with four projections wq, wk, wv, wo and a preallocated KV cache.
  • FeedForward, L307 — the SwiGLU MLP. Its entire forward pass is one line: w2(F.silu(w1(x)) * w3(x)), with the hidden dimension rounded up to a multiple of 256.
  • RMSNorm, L34 — root-mean-square normalization, x * rsqrt(mean(x²) + eps) with a learned scale, computed in float32 and cast back. No mean subtraction, no bias — that is the whole layer.
  • Tokenizer, L14 — a thin wrapper over SentencePieceProcessor that records bos_id, eos_id, and pad_id at load time and exposes exactly two methods.
  • Llama.build, L53 — the static factory that initializes the NCCL process group, globs *.pth checkpoint shards, reads params.json, and loads the state dict into a freshly constructed Transformer.
  • generate, L130 — the decode loop: pad the batch to a rectangle, call the model once per position window, sample the next token, and track which rows have hit EOS.
  • chat_completion, L284 — the chat API that validates role-alternating dialogs, folds system prompts into <<SYS>> blocks, renders the [INST] template, and then delegates to generate.

One model.py, Four Ideas

The elegance of llama/model.py is that it contains only the ideas the Llama 2 paper actually requires. The TransformerBlock, L351 is a textbook pre-norm residual: h = x + attention(norm(x)) followed by out = h + feed_forward(norm(h)). There is no dropout, no bias term anywhere in the linear layers, and no separate embedding scaling. The block is instantiated n_layers times (32 for 7B) and stacked.

Grouped-query attention is the most cited architectural change from Llama 1, and in this codebase it is disarmingly small. The attention module computes n_rep = n_local_heads // n_local_kv_heads, and a helper called repeat_kv, L164 expands each key/value head n_rep times along the head axis using expand and reshape — no copied memory, just a view trick. The 70B model uses 8 KV heads against 64 query heads, which shrinks the KV cache by a factor of 8 relative to full multi-head attention. Because the cache tensors cache_k and cache_v, L236 are allocated once in __init__ at (max_batch_size, max_seq_len, n_local_kv_heads, head_dim), that memory saving applies for the entire process lifetime, not per request.

Positional information arrives through rotary embeddings. precompute_freqs_cis, L80 builds a complex64 table of unit-magnitude complex exponentials once at construction, and apply_rotary_emb, L132 reinterprets the query and key tensors as complex numbers and multiplies them by the broadcast table. The comment above the call site in the Transformer constructor is worth reading: the table is sized to max_seq_len * 2 because the Llama 2 token limit is 4096 and the authors wanted headroom for fine-tuning at longer lengths.

The Tokenizer and the Checkpoint Loader

llama/tokenizer.py is the smallest module and the easiest to underestimate. Tokenizer.encode, L38 piece-encodes a string and optionally prepends BOS or appends EOS; Tokenizer.decode, L58 goes the other way. The constructor asserts that the SentencePiece vocab size matches the piece count and logs the special-token IDs. Everything chat-related later — stopping conditions, prompt template boundaries — leans on the bos_id/eos_id pair captured here.

The loader inside Llama.build, L53 encodes several assumptions worth noticing. It globs *.pth files in the checkpoint directory and asserts that the shard count equals model_parallel_size — the 7B model ships one shard (model-parallel degree 1), 13B ships two, and 70B ships eight, per the README’s table. Each rank reads only its own shard with torch.load(..., map_location="cpu"), then params.json hydrates a ModelArgs instance, the tokenizer’s word count overrides vocab_size, and model.load_state_dict(checkpoint, strict=False) fills the freshly built module. The strict=False is there because the checkpoint contains no freqs_cis buffer — that tensor is computed, not trained. Finally, torch.set_default_tensor_type(torch.cuda.HalfTensor) flips every subsequent allocation to CUDA fp16, a now-deprecated idiom that dates the file precisely.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s quick start is honest about the one thing you cannot get from GitHub: the weights. Installing the package itself is trivial because a setup.py exists at the repo root and declares the contents of requirements.txt (torch, fairscale, fire, sentencepiece):

pip install -e .

The weights are gated. You request access on the Meta website, accept the license, and receive a signed, expiring URL by email. That URL is fed to ./download.sh in the repository root, a wget/md5sum script that fetches the .pth shards and the tokenizer.model file for whichever models you selected. (Hugging Face mirrors exist under the same license terms.) Once the checkpoints are on disk, the README’s canonical invocation is:

torchrun --nproc_per_node 1 example_chat_completion.py \
    --ckpt_dir llama-2-7b-chat/ \
    --tokenizer_path tokenizer.model \
    --max_seq_len 512 --max_batch_size 6

example_chat_completion.py, L11 is a Fire CLI that calls Llama.build and then runs six hard-coded dialogs through chat_completion, including one deliberately unsafe prompt containing [INST] tags to demonstrate the special-tag rejection path. For base (non-chat) models, example_text_completion.py, L9 follows the identical pattern with text_completion and a few-shot translation prompt.

Sampling, Stopping, and the Chat Template

The decode loop in generate deserves attention because so many later frameworks reimplemented it line for line. Prompts of different lengths are right-padded into one rectangle; then, for each position from the shortest prompt to total_len, the model runs a forward pass over the not-yet-consumed slice. When temperature > 0, the logits are softmaxed with the temperature and passed to sample_top_p, L398, which sorts probabilities descending, zeroes tokens beyond the cumulative top-p mass, renormalizes, and draws from a multinomial. At temperature = 0 it is a plain argmax. Two subtleties stand out: tokens already belonging to the prompt are never overwritten (the input_text_mask guard), and generation stops per row, with the loop breaking only when every row has produced EOS.

The chat format lives in the same file, just above the Llama class: B_INST, E_INST = "[INST]", "[/INST]" and B_SYS, E_SYS = "<<SYS>>\n", "\n<</SYS>>\n\n". chat_completion, L284 enforces strict role alternation with assertions, merges a leading system message into the first user turn, then encodes each exchange with the template and BOS. Any user content containing the special tags is flagged and answered with an error string rather than being forwarded to the model — a tiny, instructive piece of in-band prompt-injection defense.

The detail graph: how ModelArgs configures the Transformer, how the Attention block consumes RoPE tables and the preallocated KV cache, and how Llama.build, generate, and the chat template connect the modules to the torchrun examples and download.sh.

Honest Limits

The reference code is a teaching artifact, and reading it with production eyes reveals its boundaries quickly. Every rank assumes exactly one CUDA device — torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank) runs unconditionally, the KV caches are allocated with .cuda() in __init__, and the process group is NCCL, so there is no CPU or Apple Silicon path in this code. The chat template is implemented only for the chat-finetuned checkpoints; feeding a base model through chat_completion will run, but the [INST] wrapping is a no-op semantically and will degrade output quality, which is why the separate text_completion API exists.

The KV cache, though preallocated efficiently, is not reusable across requests: each generate call writes keys and values from position zero, and nothing is carried between calls, so serving many short conversations pays full prompt processing each time. State-of-the-art serving engines rebuilt this part first. Finally, the repository itself is superseded — the README’s deprecation notice points to llama-models for Llama 3-era weights and the wider Llama Stack repos, so treat this main branch as frozen history. If you want to see where the ideas landed next, the llama.cpp project re-implemented the same architecture in pure C++ with quantization, vLLM redesigned the KV cache for continuous batching, and the PyTorch APIs used here — load_state_dict, ModuleList, torch.inference_mode — remain the substrate everything above rests on. For the tokenization side, the SentencePiece approach contrasted here with byte-level BPE is covered in our tokenizers tour.

entry.title: Megatron-LM: A Source Tour of NVIDIA’s Large-Scale Training Framework

link.title: Megatron-LM: A Source Tour of NVIDIA’s Large-Scale Training Framework

entry.content:
Megatron-LM is NVIDIA’s reference implementation for training large language models on clusters of GPUs, and it is the codebase behind many of the record-setting scaling results you see in model announcements. The repository actually ships two things: Megatron-LM, a set of pre-configured training scripts, and Megatron Core, a composable library of GPU-optimized building blocks that other frameworks (including NeMo) build on. If you have ever wondered how a model with hundreds of billions of parameters can be split across thousands of devices without the code turning into an unreadable mess, this is the place to look.

The remarkable thing about the source is how much of the magic reduces to one idea: everything is a process group. Tensor parallelism, data parallelism, context parallelism, and even the sharded optimizer are all just different ways of slicing ranks into groups and agreeing on which collective to run over which group. Once you internalize that, the code stops being intimidating. In this tour we read the actual files — the group bookkeeping in parallel_state.py, the communication primitives in mappings.py, the sharded linear layers, the transformer stack, the distributed optimizer, and the training loop that ties it all together.

We focus deliberately on tensor and sequence parallelism, the transformer implementation, and the optimizer. Megatron also contains sophisticated stage-wise 1F1B scheduling machinery, but that subsystem lives in files outside this tour’s path, so we mention it only where the code forces us to.

The overview map: CLI arguments feed the training loop; process groups back every collective; column- and row-parallel layers compose into the transformer stack that the loop trains, with sharded optimizer state stepping the gradients.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • parse_args, L130 — the single argparse entry point that collects every flag from grouped config factories.
  • validate_args, L421 — derives data-parallel size from world size and asserts the world divides evenly.
  • initialize_model_parallel, L630 — carves the tensor, context and data process groups every later collective relies on.
  • copy_to_tensor_model_parallel_region, L496 — the identity forward / all-reduce backward glue for column-parallel inputs.
  • ColumnParallelLinear, L1107 — the GEMM whose weight matrix is split along the output dimension.
  • MLP, L157 — the fc1/fc2 pair that shows the two parallel layer types working together.
  • SelfAttention, L1813 — routes QKV and output projections through the same parallel machinery.
  • train, L4552 — the top-level loop that owns iterations, logging, checkpointing and evaluation.

Process Groups: The Coordinate System

Start with megatron/core/parallel_state.py, because every other file imports it. The module is essentially a registry of process groups: tensor-parallel, data-parallel, context-parallel, and combinations of those, each stored as a global that gets initialized exactly once per process. The workhorse is initialize_model_parallel, which takes the requested sizes and computes which ranks sit in which group. Rank layout matters more than it sounds: Megatron packs tensor, context and data parallel ranks into each node so that the fastest interconnect (NVLink) carries the chattiest collectives.

The accessor functions read like a map of the design space — get_tensor_model_parallel_world_size, context- and data-parallel equivalents, and group getters for every collective type. Teardown is symmetric via destroy_model_parallel, which recent versions carefully null out to keep repeated initialization in tests honest. The recent codebase has also consolidated much of this bookkeeping into a ProcessGroupCollection object that gets passed explicitly instead of relying purely on globals — a quiet but meaningful refactor for anyone embedding Megatron Core in another framework.

The Tensor-Parallel Primitives

The actual math of tensor parallelism lives in megatron/core/tensor_parallel/. Two files do the heavy lifting. mappings.py defines the autograd-aware collectives: copy_to_tensor_model_parallel_region is a forward identity whose backward all-reduces gradients across the tensor group, and its mirror gather_from_sequence_parallel_region all-gathers inputs along the sequence dimension and scatter-reduces gradients back. That second primitive is what makes sequence parallelism work: with the flag on, layer norms and dropout operate on sequence-sharded activations, and the gathers happen exactly at the boundaries where the parallel GEMMs need full rows.

The GEMMs themselves live in layers.py. ColumnParallelLinear splits the weight along its output dimension, so each rank computes a slice of the output features from the full input; RowParallelLinear splits along the input dimension and all-reduces partial sums at the end. Chaining a column layer into a row layer — the classic Megatron trick — means one all-reduce per MLP or attention block instead of one per matrix multiply. Both layers funnel through LinearWithGradAccumulationAndAsyncCommunication, a custom autograd Function that overlaps weight-gradient accumulation with the collectives and handles sequence-parallel input gathering transparently.

The Transformer Stack

With the primitives in place, the transformer files read almost like pseudocode. megatron/core/transformer/mlp.py defines MLP: a ColumnParallelLinear fc1, a fused GELU (see the bias_gelu_impl call at L311), and a RowParallelLinear fc2. Gated variants (SwiGLU and friends) swap the activation for a tripled intermediate size and a multiplication. Note the naming drift from older releases: this class is now MLP, not the historical ParallelMLP.

attention.py is one of the largest files in the tree. The abstract Attention base wires up projections and holds the shared plumbing, while SelfAttention builds the packed QKV column-parallel projection and the row-parallel output projection. The core math delegates to dot_product_attention.py, whose DotProductAttention dispatches to fused backends — the local PyTorch path, or the TransformerEngine fused and FlashAttention kernels when available. Variants like multi-latent attention subclass the same scaffolding, which is why the file grew protocol-style builder interfaces: the class you get is resolved from a submodule spec, not hardcoded.

Stacking happens in two files. TransformerLayer sequences the pre-norm attention branch and MLP branch with residual connections and dropout, and TransformerBlock materializes the list of layers from a ModuleSpec and runs them. The spec indirection is the extension point: model files under megatron/core/models/ declare which implementations (TransformerEngine or native) each sublayer should use, which is how GPTModel assembles itself from the same block.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation follows the README. The library is on PyPI:

uv pip install megatron-core

or, if you want the training scripts and to read the source alongside:

git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM.git
cd Megatron-LM
uv pip install -e .

The README warns that building from source is memory-hungry and suggests capping compile parallelism with MAX_JOBS=4 if the build runs out. Most production users instead start from the NVIDIA GPU Cloud PyTorch container, where the CUDA toolchain and TransformerEngine are preinstalled; the official installation guide walks through that route.

The entry script is pretrain_gpt.py at the repo root. A minimal two-GPU tensor-parallel run looks like:

torchrun --nproc-per-node 2 pretrain_gpt.py \
  --tensor-model-parallel-size 2 \
  --sequence-parallel \
  --micro-batch-size 2 \
  --global-batch-size 32 \
  --num-layers 12 \
  --hidden-size 1024 \
  --num-attention-heads 16 \
  --seq-length 2048 \
  --use-distributed-optimizer

Every flag here is real: the parallel sizes come from the ModelParallelConfig dataclass that argparse factories expose as CLI options, the model geometry comes from TransformerConfig fields, and --use-distributed-optimizer is defined explicitly in megatron/training/arguments.py. In practice you would add dataset, tokenizer, and checkpoint flags — the README’s quickstart link covers data preparation — but this much already exercises the whole parallel stack from the diagrams above.

Sharded Optimizer State and the Training Loop

The optimizer subsystem is where Megatron’s memory engineering pays off. megatron/core/optimizer/optimizer_config.py defines OptimizerConfig, a dataclass holding learning rate, clipping, weight decay, and precision options. The factory get_megatron_optimizer inspects that config plus the model’s parameter groups and decides which wrapper to build. With the distributed flag on, you get DistributedOptimizer, which partitions the exp_avg and exp_avg_sq moment buffers across the data-parallel group instead of replicating them on every rank — roughly an 8x cut in optimizer memory per GPU at large DP counts compared with naive replication, and the reason the flag is on in essentially every real config.

The surrounding pieces matter too. megatron/core/distributed/distributed_data_parallel.py implements gradient bucketing with overlap of the reduce and accumulation, and finalize_model_grads (L651 in megatron/core/distributed/finalize_model_grads.py) is the hook that all-reduces gradients across data-parallel ranks and syncs embedding gradients between the ranks that own the input and output word embeddings when those live on different model stages.

On top of all this, megatron/training/training.py is the orchestration layer: setup_model_and_optimizer builds model, DDP wrapper and optimizer in one call; train owns the iteration loop, timers, logging and fault-tolerant checkpointing; train_step runs one forward-backward cycle through a user-supplied forward_step_func; and evaluate_and_print_results handles validation passes. The loop is deliberately framework-neutral about what happens inside a step — that is how the same engine drives GPT, multimodal, and hybrid architectures.

Honest Limits

A few caveats worth stating plainly. First, this is a multi-node-first framework: the abstractions assume an NCCL-capable cluster, and running on a single GPU or a laptop is possible but exercises none of the interesting machinery — if that is your situation, a smaller trainer is a better teacher. Second, the setup experience is Docker/NGC-centric; building from source works, but the pinned CUDA, NCCL and TransformerEngine versions make bare-metal installs fiddly. Third, Megatron Core is tightly coupled to TransformerEngine for its fastest paths — the fused kernels and FP8 support assume TE containers, so plans to swap in other kernel libraries need spec-level work.

Fourth, the stage-wise 1F1B scheduling machinery (interleaved schedules, microbatch splitting) is a major part of why Megatron scales, and this tour deliberately stayed out of those files; treat the diagrams here as covering the tensor-, sequence- and data-parallel story only. Finally, the codebase moves fast — classes get renamed (the old ParallelMLP is now MLP), argument groups get refactored into config dataclasses, and line numbers drift, so anchor links in older write-ups decay faster than in most projects.

The detail map adds the surrounding machinery: RNG tracking for consistent dropout, vocab-parallel cross entropy, the optimizer wrapper hierarchy, DDP bucketing and gradient finalization, and the GPT model assembly driven by layer specs.

If you want to go deeper, three adjacent reads pair well with this one: our DeepSpeed tour covers the data-parallel and sharded-optimizer alternatives from Microsoft’s side, the FlashAttention breakdown explains the kernels Megatron’s attention backend calls into, and the transformers piece covers the Hugging Face ecosystem that Megatron Bridge now converts checkpoints to and from. For a minimal contrast on how far you can get without any of this machinery, see nanoGPT. Megatron-LM is what those ideas look like when they grow up to fill a datacenter.
entry.summary: Walk through the Megatron core source: tensor and sequence parallel primitives, the transformer stack, sharded distributed optimizer, and the training entry loop.

entry.title: PaddleOCR: A Source Tour of the Multilingual OCR Toolkit

link.title: PaddleOCR: A Source Tour of the Multilingual OCR Toolkit

entry.content:
Optical character recognition looks deceptively simple from the outside — an image goes in, a string comes out — but the systems that make it work reliably are chains of specialized neural networks. PaddleOCR, the OCR toolkit from Baidu’s PaddlePaddle team, is one of the most starred OCR projects on GitHub because it packaged that full chain: a text detector that finds where the words are, a direction classifier that figures out whether a line is upside down, and a recognizer that turns cropped line images into characters across dozens of writing systems, with pretrained models in more than 80 languages.

This post is a source tour, not a tutorial. We read the code on the main branch as it exists today, after the 3.x restructure that turned the project from a pile of training scripts into a proper installable Python package. The new paddleocr package sits on top of the PaddleX inference runtime and exposes a small, tidy API, while the older training-era code still lives under ppocr/ and tools/. That duality is the most interesting thing about the current tree: you can watch a project mid-migration, with a clean wrapper layer at the front and battle-tested modeling code behind it.

We will walk the repository from the public API inward: first the package surface and the CLI, then the DB text detector with its differentiable binarization head, then the CRNN- and SVTR-style recognition stack, and finally the end-to-end det→cls→rec flow that stitches all three stages together — both in the new package and in the legacy 2.x inference scripts that still ship in tools/infer/. Two diagrams generated from the actual module graph anchor the tour.

Overview of the PaddleOCR 3.x package: the public API in paddleocr/__init__.py, the per-model wrappers, and the runtime plumbing they share.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • PaddleOCR, L36 — the one class most users ever import. The package’s __init__ re-exports it along with every standalone model class, so from paddleocr import PaddleOCR is the entire integration surface for most projects.
  • TextDetection, L27 and TextRecognition, L30 — the two stages of the OCR chain, exportable as independent models if you want to run detection without recognition or vice versa.
  • class TextDetection, L24 — the DB-style detector wrapper. In 3.x this is a thin subclass over the shared predictor wrapper, not a reimplementation of the network.
  • class TextRecognition, L23 — the recognizer wrapper, same pattern: model naming, download and predictor construction are inherited, only model-specific defaults differ.
  • TextLineOrientationClassification, L21 — the line-level 0/180° classifier that rescues text detected upside down.
  • PaddleXPredictorWrapper, L30 — the shared base class that owns predictor lifecycle, so each model file stays short.
  • parse_common_args, L38 — resolves device, precision, TensorRT and MKLDNN options into the engine config that prepare_common_init_args hands to the predictor.
  • TextSystem, L48 — the legacy 2.x orchestrator, still in the tree, which chains detector, angle classifier and recognizer by hand.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is two package names. The engine comes first, then the toolkit:

python -m pip install "paddleocr[all]"

The [all] extra pulls in the document-parsing dependencies; a minimal recognition-only install needs far less. The quick-start documentation in the repo (docs/quick_start.en.md) shows the canonical first run:

from paddleocr import PaddleOCR

ocr = PaddleOCR(
    use_doc_orientation_classify=False,
    use_doc_unwarping=False,
    use_textline_orientation=False)

result = ocr.predict("./general_ocr_002.png")

The three boolean flags are a map of the OCR chain: use_doc_orientation_classify enables a whole-page rotation model (the DocImgOrientationClassification, L21 wrapper), use_doc_unwarping enables curved-document correction, and use_textline_orientation enables the per-line 0/180° classifier. Disable all three and predict runs pure detection plus recognition — the fastest path, and the clearest view of the core det→rec flow.

The same job from the shell:

paddleocr ocr -i ./general_ocr_002.png \
    --use_doc_orientation_classify False \
    --use_doc_unwarping False \
    --use_textline_orientation False

The CLI is built in paddleocr/_cli.py: a root argparse parser registers one subcommand per model class, each contributed through the abstract base at CLISubcommandExecutor, L18. That is why paddleocr text_detection and paddleocr text_recognition work as standalone commands — every wrapper registers itself, and the CLI never hardcodes a model list. Notably, recent releases let those subcommands run with --engine transformers, executing some models through the Hugging Face stack instead of PaddlePaddle.

The first predict() call triggers model downloads: the runtime resolves a model name to a hosted archive, fetches and unpacks it into a cache directory, and only then constructs the predictor. Engine defaults such as DEFAULT_DEVICE, DEFAULT_PRECISION and the MKLDNN cache size live in paddleocr/_constants.py, L15, so tuning startup behavior on CPU-only machines is a matter of the device and enable_mkldnn arguments rather than source edits.

Text Detection: Differentiable Binarization

PaddleOCR’s default detector is a DB — differentiable binarization — network, and the clearest way to understand DB is to read its head. The modeling code behind it lives under ppocr/modeling/, the training-era half of the repo:

  • class DBFPN, L116 — the feature-preserving FPN neck that fuses multi-scale backbone features; detection needs both fine strokes and paragraph-scale context.
  • class DBHead, L168 — produces three maps: a probability map from the binarize head (built at L180), a threshold map from the thresh head, and approximate binary maps computed by the step_function at L215.

The trick in the name: classic segmentation methods threshold a probability map at the end, a non-differentiable step that pushes all supervision through one hard bottleneck. DB instead learns the threshold itself and makes the binarization step soft inside the network, so both maps get gradient signal during training. The loss that does it, class DBLoss, L29, combines Dice loss on the probability map with an L1-style loss on the threshold map.

At inference the maps become rectangles. class DBPostProcess, L29 thresholds the probability map, runs boxes_from_bitmap, L109 to find contours, “unclips” each polygon outward to recover the full text region that the shrink-map training target deliberately under-covers, and rescales coordinates back to the original image. Curved text polygons are filtered through locality-aware NMS in ppocr/postprocess/locality_aware_nms.py, which merges overlapping boxes in a way that respects their shape rather than treating them as axis-aligned rectangles.

The legacy inference script TextDetector, L36 shows exactly how these pieces connect at runtime: it wires postprocess_params["name"] = "DBPostProcess" at L77, loads the exported static model, and returns boxes plus scores. If your task needs boxes around things that are not text, the same detect-then-crop shape appears throughout vision — see our YOLOv5 tour for the object-detection cousin.

Recognition Heads: From CRNN to SVTR

Recognition is the older art here, and the repo preserves its whole evolution. The classic CRNN recipe still backs the default Chinese models: a CNN backbone turns a cropped line image into a feature sequence, a sequence neck flattens it, and a linear head classifies every timestep against a dictionary. Three files tell that story:

  • class Im2Seq, L33 — the “image to sequence” step, with BidirectionalLSTM, L59 as the context encoder that made CRNN CRNN.
  • class CTCHead, L35 — a per-timestep linear classifier. Combined with CTCLoss, L23, it trains without character-level alignment: CTC sums over all monotonic alignments between the image and the label, so you never need to know which column of pixels is which letter.
  • class CTCLabelDecode, L201 — greedy decoding at inference: collapse repeated timesteps, drop the blank symbol, then map indices through a dictionary. The parent class BaseRecLabelDecode, L23 carries the character-map plumbing; the default Chinese dictionary ships as ppocr/utils/ppocr_keys_v1.txt, a roughly 6,600-character table that defines what the model can possibly output.

The modern upgrade is SVTR — a single-visual-model recognizer that borrows the ViT recipe for text. class SVTRNet, L419 mixes local convolutional blocks with global attention blocks, keeping CNN speed where locality suffices and spending transformer capacity on full-line context. Configurations like configs/rec/rec_svtrnet.yml select it like any other backbone, because class BaseModel, L27 assembles backbone, neck and head from a YAML architecture description.

The det→cls→rec Chain, Old and New

Both generations implement the same three-step dance, but the legacy scripts make it wonderfully explicit. TextSystem, L48 constructs a TextDetector, a TextClassifier (the angle model, defined at L38) and a TextRecognizer (L39), and its __call__ at L76 reads like pseudocode: detect boxes, crop each region, flip the crops the classifier flags as upside down, batch them through the recognizer, then sort detections top-to-bottom before joining the strings.

The 3.x package implements the identical logic behind the PaddleOCR class, which composes the same three model wrappers plus optional document-level preprocessing. The stages are unchanged; what changed is who owns the plumbing. Model naming, download, predictor construction and result formatting moved into the shared wrapper layer, and legacy option names survive through shims like warn_deprecated_param, L36, which translate old kwargs while printing a migration warning instead of failing.

The detail view: the 3.x package on the left, the legacy 2.x infer chain on top, and the shared modeling, postprocess and training code underneath.

Weights, Checkpoints and the Static Graph

Because the training code still lives in-tree, you can follow a model from YAML config to deployed artifact without leaving the repository. A training run enters through main, L46, builds the architecture via BaseModel, and iterates loaders built by build_dataloader, L83 over datasets read by class SimpleDataSet, L172, which applies the imaug augmentation chain per sample. Checkpointing goes through load_pretrained_params, L199 and save_model, L241, and main, L28 freezes the trained dynamic graph into the static model files that both generations of predictors actually execute.

That static-graph contract is also the portability story. The documentation describes converting exported models to ONNX, after which they run anywhere ONNX does — our ONNX and ONNX Runtime tours cover that side of the fence. The pretrained models fetched on first run are exactly these exported artifacts, hosted centrally so users never touch the training stack.

Honest Limits

  • Chinese and English come first. The default PP-OCR models are trained primarily on Chinese and English, and the default Chinese recognizer’s output space is bounded by its ~6,600-character dictionary. Dozens of other languages ship dedicated dictionaries and models, but quality varies considerably by script, and some require a non-default lang parameter.
  • 3.x broke the 2.x API. The old ocr.ocr() call is deprecated, use_angle_cls became use_textline_orientation, the det/rec/cls boolean flags became per-feature options, and the result format changed from nested lists to dict-style objects. The shims translate and warn, but real code needs editing — the legacy scripts in tools/infer/ remain the reference for old behavior.
  • The PaddlePaddle runtime is the price of admission. The core path requires PaddlePaddle, a full deep-learning framework that dwarfs the OCR package itself. The newer --engine transformers option covers some models without Paddle, but only partially.
  • First run is a download event. Each stage of the chain — document orientation, unwarping, detection, line classification, recognition — triggers its own model fetch, so a fully enabled setup pulls several archives before the first result appears. Air-gapped environments must pre-seed the model cache by hand.

For text specifically, though, the package remains the strongest open-source starting point we know: the detection stack is genuinely good at scene text, the multilingual model zoo is unmatched in breadth, and — as this tour shows — the whole chain is readable in an afternoon. If your boxes contain objects rather than letters, YOLOv5 is the sibling tool; if you want the exported models on the cheapest possible hardware, start with ONNX Runtime or ncnn; and our Transformers tour pairs naturally with the --engine transformers story above.

entry.title: Segment Anything: A Source Tour of Meta’s Promptable Vision Model

link.title: Segment Anything: A Source Tour of Meta’s Promptable Vision Model

entry.content:
The Segment Anything Model (SAM) is Meta AI’s answer to a simple but stubborn question: can a vision model segment any object in any image, given only a hint about what to look for? Published by the facebookresearch team in 2023, SAM was trained on the SA-1B dataset — 11 million images carrying 1.1 billion masks — and it generalizes to objects and image styles it never saw during training. Instead of predicting a fixed vocabulary of classes, SAM is promptable: you give it a click, a box, or a rough mask, and it returns precise object boundaries, class-agnostic and zero-shot.

What makes the repository unusually pleasant for a source tour is its size and discipline. The whole model lives in a handful of Python files under segment_anything/, written in plain PyTorch with almost no framework magic. There are exactly three neural components — a vision transformer image encoder, a prompt encoder, and a mask decoder — plus a thin Sam container, an interactive predictor, and an automatic mask generator that orchestrates the same pieces at scale. Every module is importable, readable in one sitting, and separated from the others by clean interfaces.

This post walks through that source the way we tour other inference stacks on this blog: first a structural map, then each subsystem with real line anchors, then a runnable setup, and finally an honest account of where the model hurts. If you have read our pieces on PyTorch internals before, the shapes and tensor plumbing here will feel familiar.

Overview of the SAM repository: the encoder consumes the image once, the prompt encoder turns clicks and boxes into tokens, and the mask decoder fuses both sides to emit candidate masks.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Sam, L18 — the container module that owns all three submodules and runs the full image-plus-prompt forward pass in one call.
  • ImageEncoderViT, L17 — the heavyweight: a masked-autoencoder-style ViT that turns a 1024×1024 image into a 64×64 embedding grid.
  • PatchEmbed, L364 — the strided convolution that chops the image into 16×16 patches and adds positional embeddings.
  • Block, L119 — the transformer block, which switches between cheap windowed attention and expensive global attention by layer index.
  • PromptEncoder, L16 — converts points, boxes, and masks into sparse and dense token embeddings.
  • MaskDecoder, L16 — a deliberately lightweight transformer that fuses image and prompt tokens and emits masks plus quality scores.
  • TwoWayTransformer, L16 — the decoder’s core, where image tokens attend to prompts and prompts attend back to the image.
  • SamPredictor, L17 — the user-facing wrapper that caches encoder output so repeated prompts cost almost nothing.
  • sam_model_registry, L47 — the dict that maps vit_b, vit_l, and vit_h checkpoint names to builder functions.

A ViT Encoder That Runs Once Per Image

The encoder is where nearly all of SAM’s compute lives, and the design is a direct descendant of MAE pretraining. ImageEncoderViT takes a 1024×1024 RGB tensor, splits it with PatchEmbed into 4096 patch tokens of dimension 1280 (for ViT-H), and runs them through 32 transformer blocks. The key engineering trick is in Block: most layers use windowed attention over 14×14-token windows, and only four layers — those listed in global_attn_indexes — attend across the whole feature map. The helpers window_partition and window_unpartition do nothing more glamorous than reshaping the 64×64 token grid into 16 batched windows of 196 tokens and back again, but that reshape is what turns quadratic global attention into per-window attention for 28 of the 32 layers.

The output of the final block is a 64×64×1280 feature map that the neck at line 88 compresses with two rounds of convolution plus LayerNorm2d into 64×64×256 channels. That 256-channel embedding is the currency of the whole system: the decoder reads it, the prompt embeddings are shaped to match it, and the predictor caches it. Because the encoder is so expensive relative to everything downstream, SAM’s API is built around a hard split — encode once per image, then decode as many masks as you like. The SamPredictor exists precisely to make that split ergonomic.

From Install to Your First Model

Install directly from GitHub with pip:

pip install git+https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything.git

Then download the largest checkpoint, sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth (about 2.4 GB), from https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/segment_anything/sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth — the registry treats the string "vit_h" and the alias "default" identically. A complete interactive session, verified against the README and the SamPredictor.predict signature in predictor.py, looks like this:

import numpy as np
from segment_anything import sam_model_registry, SamPredictor

sam = sam_model_registry["vit_h"](checkpoint="sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth")
sam.to("cuda")
predictor = SamPredictor(sam)

predictor.set_image(image_rgb)          # HxWx3 uint8 RGB array
masks, scores, logits = predictor.predict(
    point_coords=np.array([[500, 375]]),
    point_labels=np.array([1]),         # 1 = foreground click
    multimask_output=True,
)

set_image resizes the long side to 1024 with ResizeLongestSide, normalizes with standard ImageNet statistics, runs the encoder once, and stores the 1×256×64×64 embedding on the predictor. Every subsequent predict call skips the encoder entirely: it transforms your coordinates back to the resized frame, embeds the prompts, and runs only the decoder. With multimask_output=True the decoder returns three candidate masks — roughly whole-object, part, and subpart granularity — together with predicted IoU scores in scores, so you can pick the best candidate without any ground truth. The low-resolution logits (256×256) can be fed back as a mask_input on the next call to refine a boundary iteratively.

Prompts: Points, Boxes, and Masks as Tokens

The prompt encoder is small but full of design decisions. Points and boxes become “sparse” embeddings: _embed_points maps each click through a small MLP whose weights encode whether the point was labeled foreground or background, and _embed_boxes represents a box as just its two corner points sharing a dedicated corner embedding — the decoder learns to treat opposite corners as a bounding gesture. A padding token is appended when no points are supplied so that batches stay aligned.

Masks take a different route: _embed_masks downsamples a 256×256 low-resolution mask with convolutional layers into the same 64×64 dense grid as the image embedding, and get_dense_pe adds a sinusoidal positional encoding so the decoder knows where each dense value sits. This asymmetry — sparse tokens for geometric hints, dense tensors for spatial hints — is what lets one decoder interface accept such different prompt types. It is also why the iterative refinement trick works: the decoder’s own 256×256 output can be re-entered as a mask prompt on the next turn, giving the model a correction channel without any retraining.

The Two-Way Mask Decoder

Detail view: the decoder concatenates IoU and mask tokens with image and prompt tokens, runs the two-way transformer, then produces masks via upscaling and hypernetwork kernels.

Inside predict_masks, the decoder concatenates a learned iou_token and four mask_tokens with the image embedding and the sparse prompt tokens, then runs the TwoWayTransformer — two layers, each one a TwoWayAttentionBlock with four steps: self-attention on image tokens, image-to-prompt cross-attention, an MLP, and prompt-to-image cross-attention. The bidirectionality matters: the prompt tokens “query” the image to find the object the user meant, while image tokens attend back to prompts so the picture context informs what each token should stand for.

Mask generation then happens in two parallel branches. The upscaled embedding branch doubles the 64×64 grid twice with transposed convolutions to 256×256. The hypernetwork branch passes each mask token through its own MLP to produce a dynamic 32×32 kernel, which is multiplied against the upscaled embedding — so each candidate mask is literally a dot product between a token-conditioned filter and the image features. Meanwhile the iou_prediction_head turns the IoU token’s output into a quality estimate per mask. The whole decoder is only a few million parameters: nearly all of SAM’s capacity is parked in the encoder, exactly so this part stays fast enough for interactive use.

From Clicks to Whole-Image Coverage

The predictor and the automatic mask generator demonstrate two opposite usage modes over the same model. SamPredictor is built for a human in the loop: one set_image, then cheap per-click predict calls, optionally with a box prompt for crisper targets. SamAutomaticMaskGenerator has no human, so it manufactures prompts: generate splits the image into overlapping crops, _process_crop lays down a 32×32 grid of foreground points (1024 clicks per crop by default), predicts masks in batches through the predictor, and pushes everything through a chain of MaskData filters — stability scoring, deduplication, and small-region removal — before stitching masks back into full-image coordinates. Both paths share the same three modules; the difference is only in how prompts are sourced and how outputs are filtered.

Honest Limits

The encoder cost is the first wall. Every new image pays a full 1024×1024 ViT-H forward pass — noticeable on a laptop GPU, several hundred milliseconds on a good desktop card — and there is no video support in this repository at all: it tracks nothing across frames, and Meta’s SAM 2 lives in a separate codebase. The model also has no semantic vocabulary. Masks are class-agnostic; if you need labels you must attach your own classifier on top of each crop, or pair SAM with something like CLIP for open-vocabulary naming.

The prompt types trade off differently than newcomers expect. A single click is ambiguous, which is exactly why multimask_output defaults to true; a box prompt resolves ambiguity well but biases the mask toward the box edges; mask prompts enable iterative refinement but are limited by the 256×256 feedback resolution, so hair-thin structures can wash out over repeated refinement rounds. Finally, the ONNX export path (SamOnnxModel in segment_anything/utils/onnx.py) covers only the prompt encoder and decoder — the ViT encoder stays in PyTorch, so browser-side demos still need a server or a separately exported encoder. If you are planning production serving around ONNX, our ONNX tour and the torchvision model utilities are the natural next stops.

entry.title: SentencePiece: A Source Tour of Google’s Language-Agnostic Tokenizer

link.title: SentencePiece: A Source Tour of Google’s Language-Agnostic Tokenizer

entry.content:
Ask a Llama checkpoint what “tokenization” means and it will answer in the dialect of SentencePiece. Google’s tokenizer library — a compact C++ core with Python bindings — has quietly become the substrate under an enormous slice of modern NLP: the Llama family, T5, ALBERT, XLNet, and countless fine-tuned descendants all ship a .model file produced by spm_train. Unlike tooling that assumes spaces delimit words, SentencePiece treats the raw byte stream as the source of truth, so Japanese, Chinese, code, and English can pass through the exact same training script without a pre-tokenizer stage. That single design decision — “no language-dependent preprocessing” — is visible everywhere in the source, and it is the thread we will follow in this tour.

The repository is refreshingly small for something this load-bearing. The inference path lives in a handful of files under src/: a processor facade, a normalizer, and four interchangeable segmentation models. The training path reuses those models under the hood but adds an expectation-maximization loop, a pruning pass, and a protobuf describing every choice made along the way. The Python side is no longer the old SWIG wrapper; since v0.2.2 the binding is pybind11 (python/src/sentencepiece/sentencepiece_pybind.cc), which also explains recent niceties like NumPy output and free-threading support.

What follows is a read of that source on the master branch, guided by two diagrams. The first gives the bird’s-eye view — who calls whom, from your Python script down to the piece-to-id map. The second zooms into the lattice machinery and the unigram trainer, where the interesting algorithms live.

The overview graph: pybind11 wraps the C++ facade, the processor fans out to a normalizer plus one of four models, and the trainer side collapses everything into a serialized ModelProto.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SentencePieceProcessor::Encode, L396 — the front door: normalize the input, ask the model for pieces, then reattach character offsets to the original text.
  • Normalizer::Normalize, L88 — trie-driven character rewriting plus whitespace escaping to the U+2581 meta symbol.
  • ModelInterface::InitializePieces, L83 — walks the model’s pieces and builds the lookup tables every subclass depends on.
  • ModelInterface::PieceToId, L69 — the abacus: a flat hash map with reserved ids (<unk>, <s>, </s>, <pad>) checked first.
  • Lattice::Viterbi, L185 — the dynamic-programming core that picks the highest-likelihood split of a normalized string.
  • bpe::Model::SampleEncode, L111 — merge-based segmentation driven by a priority queue over adjacent symbol pairs.
  • UnigramTrainer::Train, L824 — seed pieces, EM sub-iterations, and pruning until the vocabulary hits its target size.

The Processor Facade: One Entry Point, Two Halves

SentencePieceProcessor is deliberately thin. Load, L100 accepts a ModelProto and wires two members: a Normalizer and a ModelInterface. From then on, Encode is just three moves — normalize, segment, repopulate. The repopulation step, PopulateSentencePieceText, L298, is the part users rarely think about but constantly benefit from: the normalizer records a norm_to_orig mapping, and this function converts piece-level positions in the normalized string back into byte offsets in the original string, filling the SentencePieceText proto with surface, begin, and end per token. Decode runs the inverse: Decode, L492 concatenates pieces, drops control tokens, expands byte-fallback tokens, and reverses the whitespace escape so you get human-readable text out.

The two halves talk through a narrow interface. The normalizer produces a string where every space is now ▁ (U+2581, “LOWER ONE EIGHTH BLOCK”), so a piece like ▁This carries its own leading boundary. The model consumes that string and returns (piece, id) pairs. Note that the processor also exposes the map directly — PieceToId, L1101 and IdToPiece — which is all the Python piece_to_id / id_to_piece helpers funnel into.

Unigram Segmentation: A Viterbi Walk Over the Lattice

The unigram model is the default model_type, and it is the most interesting file in the repo. Its premise: each piece carries a log-probability, and the best tokenization of a string is the split with maximum total likelihood. Finding that split exactly is a shortest-path problem over a lattice, and the code builds it honestly. Model::PopulateNodes, L599 runs a common-prefix search over the vocabulary and inserts a node for every piece that matches some suffix of the input.

Classic inference then walks the DAG: Lattice::Viterbi, L185 computes, for each node, the best backtrace_score over incoming edges and keeps one back-pointer per node; reconstructing from the EOS node yields the segmentation. But the hot path does not allocate a lattice at all. Model::EncodeOptimized, L796 performs the same left-to-right dynamic program with per-position hypotheses kept in flat arrays, plus score recentering to survive very long inputs, and it falls back to the classic path only when timeouts or degenerate scores appear.

The same lattice supports three more modes that matter for training-time regularization: NBestEncode enumerates the k best segmentations, and SampleEncode draws segmentations with probability proportional to their likelihood (the “subword regularization” trick that measurably improves downstream robustness). During training, Lattice::PopulateMarginal, L268 computes how often each node appears across the whole posterior — the expected counts that the EM loop consumes.

BPE Merges, Word and Character Fallbacks

BPE in this codebase is a compact lesson in data-structure choice. bpe::Model::SampleEncode, L111 first splits the input into single-character symbols linked in a doubly-linked list, then loads an “agenda” priority queue with every adjacent pair that exists in the merge table. The comparator, SymbolPairComparator, packs scores into integers for branch-free comparison — a reminder that tokenizer code is latency-sensitive. Popping the best pair merges the two symbols in place, then pushes the new neighbor pairs back onto the agenda. The same function doubles as BPE-dropout: when alpha > 0, each merge is skipped with probability alpha, and the base class shows that plain Encode is just SampleEncode(normalized, 0.0) — deterministic merges.

One subtlety worth knowing: BPE uses PieceToIdNoReserved rather than the public lookup, so control symbols like <s> can never be merged into larger pieces by accident. The word and character models are intentionally boring. word::Model::Encode, L29 looks up whitespace-delimited tokens whole, and char::Model::Encode, L29 emits one piece per character — useful baselines, and handy when a language resists subword segmentation.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above ships as a wheel; there is no compiler between you and a working model. Install, train on a plain text file, and round-trip some text:

import sentencepiece as spm

# Train a 2000-piece unigram model from a UTF-8 corpus.
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(input='input.txt', model_prefix='m', vocab_size=2000)

# Load and use it.
sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file='m.model')

print(sp.encode('hello world'))                 # [0, 1, ...] ids
print(sp.encode('hello world', return_type=str))  # ['▁hello', '▁world']
print(sp.decode(sp.encode('hello world')))      # 'hello world'
print(sp.get_piece_size())                      # 2000

The trainer call emits the two artifacts: m.model (the serialized protobuf) and m.vocab (a human-readable piece/score listing). The same train() accepts sentence_iterator and model_writer arguments, so you can train from a URL stream into a BytesIO on machines without a writable local disk. Under the Python surface, spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train maps keyword arguments onto the C++ flag parser of SentencePieceTrainer::Train, L163, and every call logs the effective trainer_spec to stderr — worth skimming once, because it is the ground truth of what your model was configured to do.

Inside the Trainer: Seeds, EM, and Pruning

The trainer’s shared plumbing lives in TrainerInterface::LoadSentences, L368: it streams input files (or an iterator), drops empty sentences, and computes the required_chars_ set from character_coverage — characters frequent enough that they must survive into the final vocabulary. A companion filter, IsValidSentencePiece, rejects candidate pieces that break whitespace rules or exceed max_sentencepiece_length.

The unigram trainer then runs its three-phase loop. First, MakeSeedSentencePieces, L223 harvests a deliberately oversized seed vocabulary from frequent substrings (or single characters for tiny corpora). Second, the EM phase alternates RunEStep, L519 — lattice-based expected counts over sampled sentences — with RunMStep, which converts those counts into fresh piece log-probs. Third, PruneSentencePieces, L601 removes the pieces whose removal degrades the corpus likelihood the least, looping until the vocabulary shrinks to vocab_size. The result is serialized by TrainerInterface::Serialize, L651 into the proto defined by sentencepiece_model.proto — a schema where ModelProto.pieces, L298 is literally the ordered id table, and trainer_spec records the training configuration forever. The default vocab_size of 8000 is declared at L57 of the proto, next to the model_type enum defaulting to UNIGRAM.

The detail graph: the inference path on the left, the lattice/Viterbi cluster and the EM-plus-pruning trainer loop on the right, both meeting at the ModelProto schema.

Honest Limits

A few constraints are structural, and knowing them up front saves hours. Building the trainers from source requires a real C++ toolchain — CMake plus a modern compiler on every platform; the pip wheels cover common Linux/macOS/Windows targets, but embedded or exotic environments must compile the core themselves. The vocabulary is fixed before training starts: you must choose vocab_size ahead of time, and the trainer will either prune down to it or refuse to run if it cannot fit required_chars and meta pieces into that budget. There is no byte-fallback by default — unless you enable the byte_fallback flag (and include the 256 byte pieces), any character outside the vocabulary collapses into <unk>, which is exactly how many older models “lose” emoji and rare scripts. Finally, whitespace handling changes round-tripping: spaces are replaced by the ▁ underscore meta symbol and a dummy prefix is typically added, so the decoded text equals the input for ordinary sentences, but pieces you inspect in logs or embeddings tables look like ▁This rather than This, and exotic whitespace configurations can surprise you if you assume byte-identical reconstruction.

Where to go next depends on what you are building. If you are comparing tokenizers as such, the Rust-based tokenizers library is the natural counterpart, and transformers glues either one onto model checkpoints. If your interest is serving models end to end, see how vllm-2 and llama.cpp-2 handle preprocessing around the weights, or how the original llama2 architecture pairs with its SentencePiece vocabulary.

entry.title: Stable Diffusion: A Source Tour of the Original Latent Diffusion Code

link.title: Stable Diffusion: A Source Tour of the Original Latent Diffusion Code

entry.content:
Every image generator you have used in the last three years — the browser apps, the commercial APIs, the open-source forks — descends from one small research repository: CompVis/stable-diffusion. In August 2022 it shipped the weights and the reference code for Stable Diffusion v1, the first text-to-image model good enough, and light enough, to run on a consumer GPU. The paper called the method latent diffusion; the code expresses it in roughly eight thousand lines of PyTorch spread across a ldm package. Unlike the giant application built on top of it — which we toured in the stable-diffusion-webui post — this repository is almost pure model: a U-Net, a variational autoencoder, a frozen text encoder, and two samplers, with no interface layer to hide the mechanics.

That directness is exactly why the source is still worth reading. Everything that later became folklore — the 64x64 latent space, the seven-and-a-half guidance scale, the fifty sampling steps, the CLIP ViT-L/14 text tower — is visible here as ordinary Python. The training objective lives in one method, the sampling loop in another, and the trick that made it cheap (running diffusion on a compressed latent instead of raw pixels) is a four-line encode call at the top of the loss function. The project is now archived and its dependency pins have aged, but the architecture it documented became the template that diffusers industrialized and that every subsequent model inherited.

This post walks the actual files: ldm/models/diffusion/ddpm.py for the objective, ldm/models/diffusion/ddim.py and plms.py for sampling, ldm/models/autoencoder.py with its encoder and decoder for the first stage, ldm/modules/attention.py for cross-attention, and scripts/txt2img.py as the entry point. All line references were checked against the current main branch. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The overview shows the full text-to-image path: a CLI entry builds the model tree from a YAML config, samplers drive the UNet through latent space, cross-attention injects CLIP text embeddings, and the VAE shuttles between pixels and latents.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The main entry, txt2img.py L98 parses prompts, seeds, and dimensions, then owns the sampling loop that tiles finished images into a grid.
  • The config loader, L49 torch-loads the checkpoint and rebuilds the model from its YAML description rather than from pickled objects.
  • The LatentDiffusion class, L424 is the centerpiece: it holds the first stage, the conditioning encoders, and the denoising UNet in one PyTorch Lightning module.
  • The DDIMSampler.sample, L57 prepares the noise schedule buffers and runs the deterministic sampling loop over timesteps.
  • The PLMSSampler, L11 offers the pseudo-linear multistep alternative that the reference script enables with --plms.
  • The UNetModel, L413 is the 860M-parameter denoiser that predicts the noise of a compressed latent.
  • The AutoencoderKL, L285 is the KL-regularized first stage compressing 512x512x3 images into 64x64x4 latents.
  • The FrozenCLIPEmbedder, L137 turns prompt text into 77x768 embedding sequences, and the CrossAttention, L152 is where those embeddings steer the UNet.

The First Stage: Compressing Pixels into Latents

The single most important design decision in this codebase is that diffusion does not happen on pixels. The paper’s authors trained a variational autoencoder to squeeze each 512x512 RGB image into a 4x64x64 tensor — an eight-times-per-side downsample — then ran the diffusion model entirely in that compressed space. Everything else in the system orbits this choice: it is why a 4 GB GPU could generate images in 2022, and why later work on speed attacked the first stage rather than the UNet.

The autoencoder itself is conventional and clean. The Encoder, L368 is a stack of ResnetBlocks, L82 and AttnBlocks, L150 that progressively halve the spatial resolution and emit two tensors, mean and logvar; sampling from that diagonal Gaussian gives the latent. The Decoder, L462 mirrors the path back to pixels. The wrapper class hides the plumbing: AutoencoderKL.encode, L324 computes the moments and samples the posterior, while AutoencoderKL.decode, L330 multiplies by a learned scale_factor before reconstruction — that single scalar matters more than it looks, because it normalizes the latent variance so the diffusion noise schedule behaves consistently. The repository also ships VQModel, L14, the quantized-codebook variant from the original latent-diffusion paper, but Stable Diffusion v1’s released weights all use the KL version.

The Training Objective: p_losses and the Simplified Loss

The diffusion machinery lives in ldm/models/diffusion/ddpm.py, a file that starts with the pixel-space DDPM base class and then extends it twice. The base DDPM class, L44 holds the beta schedule, the q_sample, L274 forward-noising helper, and an ancestral p_sample_loop, L253. LatentDiffusion, L424 subclasses it and quietly swaps the domain: where the base class noises and denoises images, the subclass does it to VAE latents.

The training step is the clearest expression of the method. In LatentDiffusion.p_losses, L1012, a batch of images is first encoded by the frozen first stage, then a random timestep is drawn, the latent is noised with q_sample, and the UNet is asked to predict the noise that was added. The loss is simply the MSE between the predicted and actual noise — the “simplified objective” from the DDPM paper. A few lines further down, an optional decoder loss lets the model fine-tune the first stage jointly. During sampling, apply_model, L891 is the funnel every sampler calls: it concatenates the conditional and unconditional batches so one forward pass serves both, then extrapolates between them — that linear extrapolation with a scale of 7.5 is classifier-free guidance in its entirety.

Cross-Attention Is How Prompts Enter

Text conditioning in this codebase is not a hack bolted onto the UNet; it is wired into the residual blocks themselves. The SpatialTransformer, L218 is inserted at chosen resolutions of the UNet — the YAML config sets use_spatial_transformer and a context_dim of 768 — and inside, each BasicTransformerBlock, L196 applies self-attention over the image’s spatial positions, then cross-attention against the text context, then a feed-forward layer. The CrossAttention.forward, L170 is eleven lines: queries come from image features, keys and values from the 77x768 text embedding, and softmax-weighted retrieval is all the “prompt understanding” there is.

The context itself is produced by the frozen CLIP text tower. FrozenCLIPEmbedder, L137 downloads openai/clip-vit-large-patch14 from Hugging Face, forces it into eval mode in freeze, L147, and its encode, L161 tokenizes prompts and returns last hidden states. Frozen means no gradients flow into it during training — text understanding is treated as a fixed, pretrained perception organ. If you want to go deeper on the encoder itself, we covered the model family in the CLIP tour, and the open-source reimplementation in OpenCLIP; the tokenizer side is the same family of tools as transformers.

Inside the UNet Backbone and the Samplers

The UNet follows the OpenAI guided-diffusion blueprint that the community now simply calls “the SD UNet”. UNetModel, L413 builds three block stacks — input, middle, output — wrapped in TimestepEmbedSequential, L74, a small dispatch wrapper that hands each block the right arguments: residuals get the timestep embedding, transformers get the text context. Timesteps enter as sinusoidal vectors from timestep_embedding, L151, expanded by a two-layer SiLU MLP at time_embed, L507. The forward pass, L710 pushes data down the input stack while saving skip connections, runs the middle block at the bottleneck, then climbs the output stack fusing those skips — a design PyTorch makes pleasantly explicit because nothing is hidden behind framework magic.

Sampling is two files of elegant arithmetic. The DDIM sampler computes a fresh schedule in make_schedule, L25, then ddim_sampling, L114 walks the reduced timestep list calling p_sample_ddim, L166, which predicts x0 from the UNet’s noise estimate and interpolates with the direction term — eta zero gives the deterministic, forty-step-capable sampler that made fast generation practical. The same file’s stochastic_encode, L207 powers img2img by noising an input latent to an intermediate step. PLMS, in plms.py, reuses the same structure but tracks previous noise predictions for a higher-order update in p_sample_plms, L173.

The detail graph separates seven bands — entry, samplers, diffusion core, UNet backbone, attention, VAE first stage, and text conditioning — with the call edges between them.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s path still works if you accept that the pins are from 2022. Create the environment from the repo’s environment.yaml or update an existing latent-diffusion one:

conda env create -f environment.yaml
conda activate ldm
pip install transformers==4.19.2 diffusers invisible-watermark
pip install -e .

Then obtain the weights. sd-v1-4.ckpt is published on the CompVis Hugging Face organization page, which requires you to accept the CreativeML OpenRAIL-M license while logged in — effectively a Hugging Face token gate — before the download link appears. Link the checkpoint into the expected location and run the reference script:

mkdir -p models/ldm/stable-diffusion-v1/
ln -s <path/to/model.ckpt> models/ldm/stable-diffusion-v1/model.ckpt
python scripts/txt2img.py --prompt "a photograph of an astronaut riding a horse" --plms

That command renders 512x512 images in fifty PLMS steps at guidance scale 7.5 — the defaults the README documents — writing PNGs with an invisible watermark under outputs/txt2img-samples. Useful flags from the same file: --ddim_steps to trade speed for quality, --scale for guidance strength, --n_samples for batch size, and --seed for reproducibility. On modern PyTorch versions the pinned dependencies can fight the system CUDA, so the smoother route today is loading the same architecture through diffusers and only returning here to read the code.

Honest Limits

Read this repository as a historical artifact, not a running system. It is explicitly archived: the last real commits are from 2022, issues are closed, and the README itself concedes that community development has moved on. The code targets the PyTorch 1.x era — torch.load without weights_only, PyTorch Lightning pinned near version 1.4, and attention written long before scaled_dot_product_attention — so installing it verbatim on current CUDA stacks is an archaeology exercise. The CLIP weights download through the Hugging Face hub with a license gate, and the checkpoint format it loads predates the safetensors push that the ecosystem adopted for supply-chain safety.

None of that diminishes its value as a reference. The training objective, the guidance splice, and the first-stage compression are stated here more plainly than anywhere else, and every subsequent text-to-image codebase is legible as a set of edits to this one. Active development lives in the community ecosystem: the stable-diffusion-webui application for end users, diffusers for library-grade usage, and the model families that followed. Treat this repo as the primary source — the place where the ideas first appeared in code you can trace line by line.
