entry.title: timm: A Source Tour of PyTorch Image Models

link.title: timm: A Source Tour of PyTorch Image Models

entry.content:
PyTorch Image Models, known to everyone simply as timm, is the library you reach for when you need a vision backbone that actually works. Started and still curated by Ross Wightman, now hosted under the Hugging Face organization, it packs hundreds of architecture families with pretrained weights, a consistent factory API, and reference training scripts that reproduce ImageNet results. What makes timm special is not the raw model count but the discipline underneath: one entry point, one registry, one weight-loading path shared by every architecture from a tiny MobileNet to a two-hundred-layer ViT.

That uniformity is deliberate engineering, and it is best understood by reading the source rather than the docs. The whole system fits in a handful of files. timm/models/_registry.py holds the registry, timm/models/_factory.py holds the public create_model entry point, and timm/models/_builder.py does the heavy lifting of construction and checkpoint loading. The models themselves live in flat per-family files: everything ViT-related in timm/models/vision_transformer.py, everything ResNet-related in timm/models/resnet.py. Below those, timm/layers provides shared primitives, and timm/data plus the root-level train.py and validate.py scripts cover the data and training sides.

This post walks those files in dependency order, with two diagrams to anchor the territory. The first diagram shows the bird’s-eye flow from a model name string to a trained, evaluated model. The second goes one level deeper into the two reference architectures. Every symbol mentioned links to the exact line in the repository at the time of writing, so you can follow along in your editor.

The timm overview: a name string enters create_model, the registry supplies the constructor and default config, the builder attaches pretrained weights, and the finished module flows into the data and training stack.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • create_model, L162 is the single front door. One function signature, one string argument, and you get a built nn.Module.
  • generate_default_cfgs, L53 expands compact config tables into full pretrained configs for every weight variant.
  • register_model, L114 is the decorator that binds each factory function into the global registry at import time.
  • build_model_with_cfg, L427 is the shared construction path every architecture funnels through.
  • load_pretrained, L158 resolves where the weights live and downloads them from the Hugging Face Hub or a URL.
  • VisionTransformer, L749 is the reference transformer class, parameterized far beyond the original paper.
  • ResNet, L452 collapses the whole ResNet family into one configurable class.
  • create_transform, L387 turns a dataset config into matching train and eval preprocessing.
  • train_one_epoch, L1548 is the reference training loop that ties data, model, optimizer, and EMA together.

One Name In, One Model Out: the Registry and the Factory

The registry is the smallest interesting file in the repo, and it solves a real problem: how do you keep hundreds of constructors discoverable without a giant if-else chain? The answer is a decorator. When any module in timm/models is imported, each factory function wrapped by register_model, L114 inserts itself into module-level dictionaries keyed by function name. Alongside the callable, the decorator stores the module it came from, so list_models, L254 can filter by module prefix such as vit or resnet.

Naming is a protocol here. Model names look like vit_base_patch16_224.in1k, and split_model_name_tag, L33 pulls them apart into an architecture half and a pretrained-tag half. The tag selects which checkpoint the default config points to. On top of that, generate_default_cfgs, L53 lets one module declare all its variants in a compact table instead of repeating URLs and input sizes for every entry. When you later ask model_entrypoint, L369 for a name, the registry hands back the exact constructor plus its defaults.

The factory layer adds argument hygiene. create_model, L162 resolves the name, then calls resolve_model_input_args, L123 to reconcile the image size, channel count, and other input traits recorded for that architecture with whatever you overrode. This is why passing img_size=384 to a fixed-resolution model fails loudly instead of producing silently broken weights. Only after those checks does create_model delegate to the builder.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting from zero to a running ViT is two commands. Install the package:

pip install timm

Then create the model and switch it to inference mode:

import timm
model = timm.create_model('vit_base_patch16_224', pretrained=True)
model.eval()

The pretrained=True flag is where the machinery from the previous section kicks in: the registry resolves the default config, the builder downloads the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub, remaps it, and loads it into the freshly constructed module. First run needs network access; afterwards the weights are cached locally.

For inference you also want preprocessing that matches what the model saw during training. timm derives it from the model itself:

from timm.data import resolve_model_data_config, create_transform
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transform = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

This returns a torchvision-compatible transform stack with the right input resolution, ImageNet channel statistics, and resize strategy for that specific checkpoint. If you have used torchvision models before, the mental model transfers directly: the difference is that timm reads the correct settings out of the model’s config instead of asking you to hardcode them.

VisionTransformer: Patch to Prediction

The detail view: how the registry feeds the builder, how the builder remaps foreign checkpoints, and how the ViT and ResNet internals share the same layer primitives and the same training loop.

vision_transformer.py is a large file, but its shape is easy to read. Input handling lives in PatchEmbed, L26, which is just a strided convolution whose kernel and stride equal the patch size: a 224-pixel image with patch size 16 becomes 196 tokens plus one class token. The VisionTransformer, L749 class then stacks its transformer Blocks, L166, each combining normalization, Attention, L43 with fused query-key-value projection, an MLP, and residual connections wrapped in DropPath, L178, the stochastic-depth trick that randomly skips the residual branch per sample during training.

The construction path is instructive. The registered entrypoint vit_base_patch16_224, L3488 calls _create_vision_transformer, L3347, which in turn calls build_model_with_cfg and, crucially, passes along two extra hooks: a weight-init function and checkpoint_filter_fn, L1926. The filter is the remapping layer. Original research checkpoints almost never match timm’s module naming: OpenAI CLIP encoders, DINOv2 backbones, and the original tensor-flower npz files all use different key layouts. The filter translates those keys, and where the checkpoint’s positional grid differs from the target, resize_pos_embed, L1441 bicubically interpolates the position embeddings to the new resolution. A legacy torch-hub path in _load_weights, L1467 handles the same job for the very old npz format.

ResNet: One Class, Many Blocks

resnet.py takes the opposite-to-ViT approach to the same problem: rather than many small classes, one ResNet, L452 class parameterizes stem style, stage depths, downsampling strategy, and attention hooks. The classic fifty-layer variant is just a call to resnet50, L1574, which fixes depth per stage at three, four, six, and three and selects the Bottleneck, L169 block: a 1x1 reduce, a 3x3 spatial conv, a 1x1 expand with expansion factor four. Shallower variants use BasicBlock, L49, two 3x3 convs with no expansion.

The block list is built by make_blocks, L363, which also distributes a linearly increasing stochastic-depth rate across blocks, reusing the same DropPath primitive the ViT uses. That reuse is the quiet thesis of the whole library: regularization techniques and layer primitives are written once in timm/layers and consumed by every architecture, which is why a ResNet trained with timm and a ViT trained with timm share the same reproducibility behavior. Pretrained weight handling flows through the identical builder path, including adapt_input_conv, L293, which converts a 3-channel stem into grayscale or hyperspectral inputs by averaging weights when you create a model with a different in_chans.

Data, Training, and the EMA Sidecar

On the data side, create_transform, L387 picks a recipe branch; the training branch in transforms_imagenet_train, L65 assembles RandAugment, color jitter, interpolation choices, and the standard ImageNet mean and standard deviation, with an eval branch that keeps only resize, crop, and normalization. The loader layer in create_loader, L223 wraps a dataset in a DataLoader using a fast collate function that produces device-friendly uint8 batches, then optionally wraps it in PrefetchLoader, L82, which moves the next batch to GPU and normalizes it asynchronously so the compute never waits on the CPU.

The training scripts now live at the repository root rather than inside the package. train_one_epoch, L1548 runs the forward pass under AMP autocast, computes the possibly mixup-blended loss, clips gradients, steps the optimizer and scheduler, and updates the EMA model. The EMA sidecar, ModelEmaV2, L85, keeps a decayed copy of the weights that typically evaluates a fraction of a point higher on ImageNet at zero extra training cost. Evaluation uses the same validate, L1772 function during training and in the standalone script, so numbers reported mid-run and post-run are directly comparable.

Honest Limits

The breadth has a price. First, pretrained coverage: timm publishes 800+ checkpoints on the Hugging Face Hub, and pulling them requires real bandwidth; first-run downloads can be gigabytes, and per-checkpoint licenses vary, so check the model card before shipping anything commercial. Second, scope: this is an image classification zoo. Detection, segmentation, and video models exist only as backbones or via adjacent projects, and if you need those tasks end to end you will be writing heads yourself. Third, the factory surface drifts between versions: create_model kwargs like drop_path_rate, img_size, and feature-extraction flags get added, renamed, or deprecated across releases, so a snippet that worked last year may need adjustment, and the upgrade notes deserve a skim before any major version bump. Finally, while weights are increasingly offered in modern container formats such as safetensors, the legacy loading path still accepts arbitrary pickled checkpoint files, which matters if you load untrusted weights. For general multimodal and text models you will end up in the neighboring transformers library, and timm’s own CLIP-family weights echo open-clip; both are complementary rather than overlapping.

If you want one takeaway: timm’s power comes from narrow, boring, consistent infrastructure. The registry makes models findable, the factory makes them constructible, the builder makes weights loadable, and the layers and data modules make training reproducible. Read those four paths once and every one of the hundreds of models becomes an open book.
entry.summary: Walk through the timm source: the create_model registry and builder, VisionTransformer and ResNet implementations, DropPath, checkpoint remapping, and the training engine.

entry.title: YOLOv5: A Source Tour of Ultralytics’ Real-Time Object Detector

link.title: YOLOv5: A Source Tour of Ultralytics’ Real-Time Object Detector

entry.content:
When YOLOv5 appeared in mid-2020, it was slightly scandalous: a “YOLOv5” with no paper behind it, built directly in PyTorch while YOLOv4 was still a Darknet project. Four years of production use later, the Ultralytics/yolov5 repository has become one of the most-forked detection codebases on GitHub, and its longevity owes much to a few legible design decisions. The repo is not a library you import so much as an application you run: train.py, val.py, detect.py, and export.py at the top level, with everything else tucked into models/ and utils/.

The most consequential of those decisions is that the network architecture is data, not code. A models/yolov5s.yaml file lists every layer of the backbone and head, and a single function — parse_model — turns that list into real PyTorch modules. That one move is what made the s/m/l/x family trivial: the same layer graph, scaled by depth and width multiples. It also explains why the repo aged well; adding a new block type meant teaching parse_model one more name, not rewriting the builder.

This post is a source tour of the current master branch. We follow the path a detection actually takes: yaml to modules in parse_model, forward through C3 and SPPF blocks into the anchor-decoding Detect head, out through non_max_suppression, and across the export surface that DetectMultiBackend loads back. Two diagrams generated from the real repository tree anchor the tour — a compact overview and a detailed call graph.

Overview graph of YOLOv5: entry points feed a yaml-driven model assembly stage, whose backbone blocks and anchor head hand raw predictions to the NMS and multi-backend runtime layer.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • parse_model, L375 — the yaml interpreter: walks the layer list, resolves repeats through depth scaling, and instantiates every module.
  • DetectionModel, L215 — wraps parse_model, probes strides with a dummy forward, and initializes head biases.
  • Detect, L71 — the anchor head: one 1×1 conv per scale, sigmoid split, and grid/anchor decoding of box coordinates.
  • SPPF, L318 — the fast spatial-pyramid-pooling block that concatenates three sequential 5×5 max-pools.
  • letterbox, L85 — aspect-preserving resize with gray padding to the model stride.
  • non_max_suppression, L658 — batched, class-aware NMS with the offset trick that keeps per-class suppression independent.
  • DetectMultiBackend, L456 — one inference interface over PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, TensorFlow, OpenVINO and friends.
  • attempt_load, L60 — the checkpoint loader that un-pickles .pt files, optionally fuses layers, and can return an Ensemble.

From Install to Your First Model

The repo is meant to be cloned and run, and the README’s quick start is genuinely two commands long. After cloning, install the pinned dependency set — the requirements file is versioned carefully because several optional accelerators (onnxruntime, TensorRT, CoreML tools) move fast:

git clone https://github.com/ultralytics/yolov5
cd yolov5
pip install -r requirements.txt

Then run inference on the bundled sample images. The first invocation downloads yolov5s.pt (6.2M parameters) automatically and writes annotated results to runs/detect/exp:

python detect.py --source data/images --weights yolov5s.pt

The same model is reachable without cloning, through the hubconf.py entry point. _create, L16 downloads the weights, loads them via attempt_load, and by default wraps the network in AutoShape so you can feed it file paths, PIL images, or NumPy arrays directly:

import torch
model = torch.hub.load("ultralytics/yolov5", "yolov5s")
results = model("https://ultralytics.com/images/zidane.jpg")
results.print()

Both paths converge on the same objects: a DetectionModel and, in the hub case, an AutoShape shell that hides the letterbox/NMS/rescale choreography from the caller.

parse_model: Architecture as Data

Open models/yolov5s.yaml and you find three sections: hyperparameters (nc, depth_multiple, width_multiple, anchor lists), a backbone list, and a head list. Each row is [from, number, module, args] — where the feature comes from, how many times it repeats, which class to build, and with what arguments. parse_model reads these rows in order, maintaining a ch list of output channels and a save list of layer indices that later layers consume via the from field.

Two global scalings make one yaml describe four model sizes. depth_multiple divides the number column, so yolov5n builds fewer Bottleneck repeats than yolov5x; width_multiple scales every channel count, shrinking or widening each conv. Repetitive blocks are handled by a dictionary of class pairs — C3 maps to (C3, [256])-style signatures — so a row like - [-1, 3, C3, [256, True]] becomes one module with n inner repeats rounded by make_divisible.

The building blocks themselves are refreshingly plain. Conv is conv-BN-SiLU with padding from autopad, which infers “same” padding from the kernel size and honors dilation. C3 is the CSP variant: two conv stems, n Bottleneck blocks in one branch, a straight conv path in the other, concat, and a 1×1 to mix. SPPF replaced the original four-parallel-kernel SPP with three chained 5×5 max-pools whose concatenated outputs cover the same receptive fields — the MAXPOOL legalization for TensorRT came as a bonus of that design.

DetectionModel orchestrates all of this: it calls parse_model, then runs a 256-pixel dummy tensor through the network to measure the stride of each Detect layer, asserts the strides divide 32 cleanly, and re-seeds head biases toward a known prior. Forward passes live in BaseModel, whose _forward_once loops over self.model, stashing outputs of saved layers so from: -1 and from: [4] style wiring works without any graph machinery. DetectionModel.fuse() folds Conv+BN pairs via fuse_conv_and_bn in utils/torch_utils.py — a real latency win at inference.

The Detect Head: Anchors, Grids, and Decoding

YOLOv5 is anchor-based — deliberately, even as anchor-free competitors multiplied — and the entire mechanism lives in about sixty lines. The head’s __init__ registers an (nl, na, 2) anchor buffer, computes na (anchors per layer, 3 by default) and no = nc + 5 outputs per anchor, then creates one nn.Conv2d(x, no * na, 1) per detection scale.

In Detect.forward, each per-scale feature map is reshaped from (bs, 255, ny, nx) to (bs, na, ny, nx, 85). During inference the tensor is split into box and class halves, and the decode happens in-place:

xy, wh, conf = x[i].sigmoid().split((2, 2, self.nc + 1), 4)
xy = (xy * 2 + self.grid[i]) * self.stride[i]
wh = (wh * 2) ** 2 * self.anchor_grid[i]

Those two lines, L109–111, are the whole anchor story: sigmoid outputs in (0,1) are stretched to (−0.5, 1.5) cells by the * 2 + grid − 0.5 affine, then multiplied by stride for centers; width and height are squared so the network predicts a multiplicative factor around the preset anchor box. The grids themselves come from _make_grid, which rebuilds meshgrid buffers whenever the input’s spatial shape changes — that check is what makes the model “dynamic” for non-square inputs. In training mode the head returns the raw per-scale tensors instead, because ComputeLoss in utils/loss.py needs the un-decoded predictions to assign targets against anchor priors.

The detect.py Flow: From Frames to Boxes

detect.run is the reference consumer of everything above, and it is worth reading top to bottom once. After argument parsing, it calls select_device and check_img_size, which rounds your requested inference size up to the nearest multiple of the model stride. Weights load through DetectMultiBackend; for .pt files that lands in attempt_load, which applies torch.load with a strict allowlist and optionally fuses Conv+BN immediately.

The source loop uses LoadImages, a generator yielding BGR frames, original-resolution copies, and video metadata across images, videos, globs, and streams. Each frame passes through letterbox, then the batched forward produces (bs, anchors, 85) predictions, which are passed to non_max_suppression — visible in context at detect.py L228.

That NMS implementation rewards a close read. It batches across the batch dimension with a confidence threshold, converts xywh to xyxy once, then — the clever part — adds a per-class offset of classes * max_wh to box coordinates so that torchvision.ops.nms never suppresses across classes, before subtracting the offset back. Box limits are clamped, max_det caps survivors per image, and an optional merge mode averages boxes weighted by IoU. The survivors are still in letterbox coordinates, so scale_boxes maps them back to original pixels using the ratio and padding recorded earlier. What remains is presentation: the Annotator draws boxes, save_crop can cut each detection out with padding — done via numpy slicing on the original frame — and increment_path allocates the next runs/detect/exp directory.

DetectMultiBackend and the Export Surface

The bridge between training and deployment is DetectMultiBackend. Its constructor dispatches purely on file suffix: .pt goes through attempt_load, .onnx builds an onnxruntime.InferenceSession with CUDA/CPU provider selection, .engine deserializes a TensorRT runtime (with a helpful error if the engine was built by a different TRT version), and .tflite, .pb, .xml (OpenVINO), CoreML, Paddle, and Triton each get their branch. Its forward normalizes everything to a single return shape, and its _model_type helper is the definitive list of what the repo can consume.

The production side is export.py. export.run loads the checkpoint, builds an example input, and calls one export function per requested format, then re-validates each artifact with DetectMultiBackend and runs a single-image sanity inference. export_onnx exports with dynamic axes when --dynamic is set and optionally runs onnx-simplifier; export_engine builds a serialized TensorRT engine with workspace and precision flags. Our onnx and tensorrt tours cover what those formats contain at the runtime level; openvino covers the .xml/.bin branch. On the training side, augmentations feed mosaicked batches, while preprocessing stays letterbox-based — a contrast worth remembering when reading torchvision detection reference code.

Detailed graph of the same tour: every node is pinned to a real file in the repository, from the yaml assembly and Detect head down to export targets and evaluation metrics.

Honest Limits

Be clear-eyed about what this codebase is in 2026. Ultralytics’ own attention has moved to the unified ultralytics package (YOLOv8 and later, anchor-free heads, integrated CLI); the yolov5 repository is in maintenance mode — still maintained, but the successor is where new research lands, and a few helpers in utils/torch_utils.py (like time_sync and model_info) are now re-imported from the installed ultralytics package.

The anchor-based design is a strength for deployment stability but a tax for new domains: the anchors in each yaml are hand-tuned for COCO-like object scales, and while check_anchors in utils/autoanchor.py can re-run k-means on your dataset, off-domain deployments (aerial imagery, elongated objects) still need anchor and threshold babysitting. The NMS defaults — conf_thres=0.25, iou_thres=0.45 — are reasonable starting points, not constants; dense or tiny-object scenes reliably demand per-domain tuning of both thresholds and max_det. Finally, the license is AGPL-3.0, which means embedding this code (or a derivative network’s training stack) in a distributed product creates source-disclosure obligations — a real consideration for commercial integration that predates but survives into the 8.x package.

None of that diminishes the engineering value of reading it. YOLOv5 remains one of the best case studies of a complete, deployable detection system whose complexity budget was spent on legibility — yaml as architecture, one head, one NMS, one loader that accepts every runtime the ecosystem produced.
entry.summary: Walk through the YOLOv5 source: parse_model yaml assembly, the Detect anchor head, non-max suppression, DetectMultiBackend export loading, and the detect.py flow.

entry.title: BERT: A Source Tour of Google’s Original Transformer Encoder

link.title: BERT: A Source Tour of Google’s Original Transformer Encoder

entry.content:
When Google published “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding” in October 2018, the paper landed together with a reference implementation — the google-research/bert repository. That repo is the artifact this tour reads. It is written for TensorFlow 1.x in graph mode, built on the Estimator API, and it carries the unmistakable texture of late-2018 research code: flag parsing at the top of every script, TPUEstimator wiring, and comments that explain not just what the code does but why the authors chose that design.

What strikes most readers first is the size. There is no package directory, no src/ tree, no build system. The whole thing is roughly a dozen files at the repository root, and the ones that matter are eight Python scripts: modeling.py, tokenization.py, run_classifier.py, run_squad.py, optimization.py, extract_features.py, create_pretraining_data.py, and run_pretraining.py. That is the complete surface area of the most influential language model of its era — the codebase that other teams ported to PyTorch, that spawned the fine-tuning ecosystem, and that turned “pre-train once, fine-tune everywhere” from an idea into an industry default.

Reading it top-down is rewarding precisely because the graph-mode style forces every tensor transformation to be explicit. Nothing hides behind an nn.Module with implicit state; you can trace a token from a raw string all the way to a probability without leaving a handful of files. This post walks that path at two zoom levels, mapped by the two diagrams below.

The overview graph: four task runners on the right pull from the tokenizer and the shared encoder; optimization is a small, self-contained module that every trainer reuses.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • BertModel, L107 is the heart of the repo. Its constructor wires the embedding lookup, the attention mask, the encoder stack, and a tanh pooler into one computation graph, then exposes accessors like get_sequence_output() and get_pooled_output() for downstream heads.
  • BertConfig, L31 is the hyperparameter record that separates BERT-Base (12 layers, 768 hidden units, 12 heads) from BERT-Large (24 layers, 1024 hidden, 16 heads), including dropout rates and the GELU activation choice.
  • FullTokenizer, L161 is the single entry point for raw text. It chains a rule-based cleaner with a subword splitter and finally maps tokens to vocabulary indices.
  • WordpieceTokenizer, L300 implements the greedy longest-match search that turns words missing from the vocabulary into ##-prefixed fragments — the detail that let a 30k-token vocabulary cover English nearly losslessly.
  • model_fn_builder, L619 returns the model_fn closure that TPUEstimator calls; it is the junction where the encoder, the task head, the loss, and the training op meet.
  • create_optimizer, L25 assembles the learning-rate schedule — linear warmup followed by polynomial decay — and clips gradients to a global norm of 1.0.
  • AdamWeightDecayOptimizer, L87 is the Adam variant with decoupled weight decay, deliberately skipping LayerNorm kernels and biases — a recipe later papers copied almost verbatim.
  • write_predictions, L741 closes the question-answering loop, joining raw start/end logits with token features to emit n-best answer strings in original text.

One File, One Encoder: modeling.py

Everything in modeling.py exists to answer one question: given input_ids, input_mask, and token_type_ids, what tensors come out? The constructor of BertModel reads like a checklist of the architecture. First, embedding_lookup, L380 maps integer WordPiece ids to dense vectors, with a one-hot matmul path kept for TPU efficiency. Then embedding_postprocessor, L428 adds learned position embeddings and segment (token-type) embeddings on top, applies LayerNorm and dropout — this is where BERT differs from the original Transformer by using learned positions rather than sinusoids.

Attention itself is split into two functions. attention_layer, L558 does one round of multi-head scaled dot-product attention: it reshapes the 768-dim hidden states into per-head slices, computes Q·Kᵀ/√d, adds the mask as an additive bias before the softmax, and projects the concatenated heads back to the model width. transformer_model, L754 is the loop that runs num_hidden_layers rounds of that attention plus a position-wise feed-forward network activated by gelu, L264. The attention mask starts life as a simple 2D padding indicator and is expanded into a 3D bias by create_attention_mask_from_input_mask, L524.

Finally, the pooler. Lines 224 through 232 squeeze out the hidden state of the first token (the [CLS] slot), push it through a dense tanh layer, and stash the result; get_pooled_output, L234 hands it to task heads, while get_sequence_output() returns the full per-token sequence for tagging and extraction.

WordPiece, With the Rules in Plain Sight: tokenization.py

The tokenizer file is the most portable code in the repo — pure Python, no TensorFlow at all. load_vocab, L121 reads vocab.txt, one token per line, into an ordered dictionary. FullTokenizer, L161 then composes two stages. Stage one is BasicTokenizer, L185: optional lower-casing and accent stripping, splitting CJK characters into singletons, and breaking punctuation into separate tokens. Stage two is WordpieceTokenizer, L300: for each word, take the longest prefix that exists in the vocabulary, mark it, then repeat on the remainder with a ## continuation marker, giving up after 100 characters and emitting the [UNK] token instead.

The output mapping happens in convert_tokens_to_ids, L144, a trivial dictionary lookup that nonetheless defines the exact integer contract every downstream consumer depends on. Because the logic is deterministic and dependency-free, this file was lifted almost unchanged into later reimplementations; its modern, fast-Rust descendant lives on in tokenizers, which still ships BERT’s original vocab format.

Two Task Scripts, One Pattern

run_classifier.py and run_squad.py share an identical skeleton: read examples, convert to fixed-length features, build a model on top of BertModel, wrap it in an Estimator, train, predict. Learning one teaches you the other, and both teach you the TF1 idiom.

In the classifier script, GLUE datasets enter through DataProcessor subclasses (MrpcProcessor, L296, XnliProcessor, L207) that yield InputExample records. convert_single_example, L377 tokenizes a sentence pair and calls _truncate_seq_pair to fit max_seq_length by trimming the longer sentence from the right; file_based_convert_examples_to_features, L479 serializes the InputFeatures, L161 records into TFRecord protos that file_based_input_fn_builder, L509 parses back inside the Estimator input function. The head is deliberately boring: create_model, L574 takes the pooled output, applies dropout, and does a single matrix multiply into a softmax.

The SQuAD script adds span logic. read_squad_examples, L227 aligns answer character offsets to whitespace tokens; convert_examples_to_features, L309 slides a doc_stride window across long passages, marking which window holds the true answer via _check_is_max_context; the model at create_model, L550 emits two logits vectors for start and end positions. Prediction time in write_predictions, L741 reassembles WordPiece output into readable text with get_final_text, L927. A third runner, extract_features.py (entry at main, L343), skips heads entirely and dumps contextual embeddings from any requested layer — still a popular way to get fixed BERT features for downstream models.

From Install to Your First Model

This is TensorFlow 1-era code, and honesty matters here: the paths below describe how the repo was meant to be run, and what it costs. The requirements.txt asks for tensorflow >= 1.11.0 (CPU build; the GPU build was a separate tensorflow-gpu package). On a modern machine the pragmatic route is a dedicated Python 3.7-or-earlier environment with the last TF1 release:

conda create -n bert-tf1 python=3.7 -y
conda activate bert-tf1
pip install tensorflow==1.15
git clone https://github.com/google-research/bert.git
python run_classifier.py --help   # sanity-check the flag surface

Then download the uncased_L-12_H-768_A-12 BERT-Base checkpoint, grab the GLUE MRPC data, and run the README’s fine-tuning example:

export BERT_BASE_DIR=/path/to/uncased_L-12_H-768_A-12
export GLUE_DIR=/path/to/glue

python run_classifier.py \
  --task_name=MRPC \
  --do_train=true \
  --do_eval=true \
  --data_dir=$GLUE_DIR/MRPC \
  --vocab_file=$BERT_BASE_DIR/vocab.txt \
  --bert_config_file=$BERT_BASE_DIR/bert_config.json \
  --init_checkpoint=$BERT_BASE_DIR/bert_model.ckpt \
  --max_seq_length=128 \
  --train_batch_size=32 \
  --learning_rate=2e-5 \
  --num_train_epochs=3.0 \
  --output_dir=/tmp/mrpc_output/

MRPC is tiny — about 3,600 examples — so this converges in roughly 343 steps and a few minutes on most GPUs, landing near 84–88% dev accuracy. The README is candid about hardware: everything runs on CPU, GPU, or Cloud TPU; BERT-Base fine-tuning fits comfortably in 12 GB of GPU memory, while BERT-Large wants 12–16 GB and will still out-of-memory on SQuAD even at batch size 1 on a 12 GB card. Pretraining from scratch is another world entirely — the paper’s BERT-Base replication took about an hour on a 16-cloud-TPU pod, and run_pretraining.py (entry at main, L406) assumes that scale, with create_pretraining_data.py (main, L436) masking 15% of tokens up front.

Honest Limits

Treat this repository as an archive, not a dependency. It is frozen TF1 code: tf.layers, Estimator, and tf.contrib calls that modern TensorFlow removed, plus Python 2/3 straddling helpers like convert_to_unicode. Nothing here has been maintained for years, and Google has long since moved on. The architecture itself was also superseded within two years — RoBERTa, ELECTRA, and DeBERTa each kept the skeleton and replaced the training recipe or the head design.

For real work today, the ecosystem lives elsewhere. Hugging Face transformers reimplements BERT in PyTorch, loads these exact checkpoints, and has become the de facto interface for the entire encoder family. The WordPiece algorithm survived as the tokenizers library in fast Rust. If you need the original frozen graph out of the TF1 world, exporting through ONNX remains the cleanest exit. What this repo still offers that no replacement can, is legibility: eight files where every design decision of the foundational era — learned positions, the [CLS] pooler, decoupled weight decay, warmup schedules — sits in plain sight with a comment above it.

The detail graph: from FullTokenizer's two stages through the encoder stack, into the classifier and SQuAD heads, with the pretraining scripts sharing the same optimizer.

If you want to go deeper, start at BertModel and follow the tensors; every symbol above links to the exact line in the upstream repository, and the repository’s README remains the best companion for checkpoint formats and hardware expectations.

entry.title: coremltools: How Apple Compiles PyTorch Models Onto the Neural Engine

link.title: coremltools: How Apple Compiles PyTorch Models Onto the Neural Engine

entry.content:
If you have ever trained a network in PyTorch and then wondered how it ends up running inside an iOS app with a 40% smaller footprint and zero Python interpreter in sight, the answer is almost always coremltools. Apple’s open-source toolkit takes a model expressed in a training framework, rewrites it into an intermediate representation called MIL (Model Intermediate Language), and serializes it into the .mlpackage format that Core ML — the on-device runtime baked into iOS, iPadOS and macOS — can load, schedule across CPU/GPU/Neural Engine, and execute natively. The repo lives at apple/coremltools, it is a large but readable Python codebase, and in this post we walk its main streets: the conversion entry point, the MIL IR, the graph passes that optimize programs, the backend that serializes them, and the post-training compression stack.

It is worth placing the tool in Apple’s ecosystem before diving into code. MLX is Apple’s NumPy-like array framework for training and research on Apple silicon — it wants to be your modeling language. coremltools is the shipping layer: it assumes you already have trained weights and cares about freezing them into a format that Xcode, CoreML.framework, and the ANE compiler stack understand. The two are siblings, not competitors, and a common workflow is train in PyTorch (or MLX, exporting through PyTorch), then hand the frozen module to coremltools.

The tour below is based on a checkout of main. We will follow one conversion end to end, look at how op coverage and deployment targets interact, run an actual ct.convert, then compress a model after the fact. Two diagrams anchor the navigation: a compact overview and a detailed graph with 21 nodes.

Overview of coremltools: user API, frontends, the MIL IR, graph passes, backend serialization, the MLModel runtime wrapper, and the post-training optimization stack.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • convert, L69 — the public ct.convert() signature: source auto-detection, inputs/outputs types, compute_units, minimum_deployment_target, and a states argument for KV-cache-style models.
  • mil_convert, L148 — the dispatcher. A ConverterRegistry maps a convert_from string (pytorch, tensorflow, tensorflow2) to a frontend class and convert_to (mlprogram, neuralnetwork) to a backend.
  • load, L27 — the PyTorch frontend’s gate: it accepts a TorchScript module, a .pt/.pth path, or a torch.export ExportedProgram, and wraps it in a TorchConverter.
  • convert_single_node, L125 — the heart of transcription: for every node in the internal torch graph it looks up a registered handler, binds scope/debug metadata, and emits MIL ops through the mb.* builder.
  • SSAOpRegistry, L17 — the versioned op registry: core_ops (keyed by opset, from iOS13 up), dialect_ops (framework-specific), and custom_ops.
  • Program, L26 — the SSA IR container that frontends emit into: functions, blocks, Vars, plus hooks for the pass machinery.
  • MILProtoExporter, L75 — the mlprogram backend: converts a PyMIL Program into the MIL protobuf, streaming large weights into external .bin files inside the package.
  • MLModel, L308 — the runtime wrapper returned to users: save, predict, compute-unit pinning, state objects, and spec introspection.
  • linear_quantize_weights, L56 — the post-training path: int8/int4 weight quantization, palettization and pruning applied to an already-converted .mlpackage.

The MIL IR: One Intermediate for Three Frontends

The design decision that shapes the whole repository is MIL: a single static single-assignment language that every frontend lowers into and every backend consumes. The Builder, L69 is what frontend code actually calls — mb.conv, mb.mul, mb.matmul — and each call resolves the correct version of the op for the deployment target you asked for. The same op name can exist at multiple opsets; the registry picks the right class from core_ops[op_type] based on the current function’s opset version. That is how one conversion target string (ct.target.iOS17, for example) changes the shape of the generated program.

Op definitions are physically organized by opset folder, which makes platform evolution easy to read in the source tree. conv, L17 subclasses the iOS15 implementation and registers itself for the iOS17 target; newer machine-learning ops live in the iOS18 folder — for instance scaled_dot_product_attention, L18, the fused attention primitive that transformer models need to avoid materializing full attention matrices on device.

The TensorFlow side reuses exactly the same IR. TF2Loader, L43 consumes Keras models, SavedModel directories, frozen graphs and concrete functions, and emits MIL just like the torch frontend does. So if your origin story is TensorFlow rather than PyTorch, the back half of the flow — passes, serialization, runtime — is byte-for-byte the same machinery. On the torch side, handlers are registered with register_torch_op, L100, which also supports aliases (one torch op kind handled by several names) and inplace variants that the context tracks so SSA semantics are preserved.

Graph Passes: Where Models Get Faster

After a frontend produces a raw MIL program, the optimization stage rewrites it in place. Every rewrite implements AbstractGraphPass, L41 — a small interface with a apply_to_program-style entry plus PassOption knobs that users can override through pass_options when calling ct.convert.

A representative example is fuse_activation_silu, L66: it pattern-matches sigmoid feeding a mul and replaces the pair with a single silu op. Fewer ops means fewer dispatches at runtime and a better shot at ANE scheduling. The same folder contains fusions for pow/sqrt chains, constant decomposition, and name sanitization. Two passes deserve special mention because they touch correctness rather than speed: adjust_io_to_supported_types, L20 casts inputs and outputs to dtypes the chosen opset actually supports (fp16 I/O for mlprogram targets, for example), and insert_image_preprocessing_ops, L18 bakes scale/bias and channel reordering into the graph when you declare an input as ct.ImageType, so the app can hand the model a raw CVPixelBuffer and get correct numbers.

Serialization then happens in the mlprogram backend. The MILProtoExporter writes per-op protobuf records, and should_use_weight_file (same file, L59) decides whether a constant is small enough to inline or big enough to stream into Weight.bin inside the package — this is the mechanism that makes multi-gigabyte LLMs storable and lazily mappable by the OS. The companion class CoreMLProtoExporter, L590 layers on the model description: input/output feature types, flexible-shape enumerations, classifier wiring, and state features.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one pip line (Python 3.9+ is what current releases target):

pip install coremltools

You will also need a PyTorch install if your source model is torch-based. The minimal flow is: script or export the module, call ct.convert with typed inputs, save the package:

import coremltools as ct
import torch

class TinyNet(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 3, padding=1)
        self.relu = torch.nn.ReLU()
        self.head = torch.nn.Linear(16 * 8 * 8, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.relu(self.conv(x))
        return self.head(torch.flatten(x, 1))

model = TinyNet().eval()
scripted = torch.jit.script(model)

mlmodel = ct.convert(
    scripted,
    inputs=[ct.TensorType(shape=(1, 3, 8, 8))],
    compute_precision=ct.precision.FLOAT16,
    compute_units=ct.ComputeUnit.ALL,
)
mlmodel.save("TinyNet.mlpackage")

ct.convert (the function at the top of the overview diagram) returns an MLModel immediately. Two arguments matter most in practice. compute_precision=ct.precision.FLOAT16 tells the converter to store and compute in half precision — the default for mlprogram targets and what the Neural Engine expects. compute_units accepts ct.ComputeUnit.ALL, CPU_ONLY, or CPU_AND_GPU; ALL lets the runtime schedule on the ANE when ops allow it. The same wrapper then loads the package and runs inference on a Mac via predict, L826 — a dict in, a dict out — which is also how you sanity-check numerics before deploying to a phone. One subtlety worth knowing: predict requires macOS 12.0+ for .mlpackage models, and the spec version you target must be supported by the Core ML framework installed on the machine.

Weight Compression After the Fact

Conversion is only half the toolkit. coremltools.optimize operates on already-converted .mlpackage models and applies post-training compression to their weight constants. The config objects live in _config.py — OpLinearQuantizerConfig, L131 exposes mode (linear_symmetric/linear), dtype (int8, int4), granularity (per_tensor, per_channel, per_block) and block_size — and the public functions linear_quantize_weights, palettize_weights, prune_weights, and get_weights_metadata are what you call from Python:

from coremltools.optimize.coreml import (
    OpLinearQuantizerConfig,
    linear_quantize_weights,
)

config = OpLinearQuantizerConfig(
    mode="linear_symmetric",
    dtype="int4",
    granularity="per_block",
    block_size=32,
)
compressed = linear_quantize_weights(mlmodel, config=config)
compressed.save("TinyNet_int4.mlpackage")

Under the hood each function instantiates a registered MIL pass — for quantization that is linear_quantize_weights, L1170 — which rewrites each weight const into a compressed constexpr_ dequantize form, so the on-device runtime materializes weights on the fly in the compute unit’s preferred format. The same registry mechanism that served conversion is reused here, which is a genuinely elegant piece of reuse. For LLM-sized models, per_block int4 is the option Apple’s own export recipes lean on: it keeps outliers tolerable by giving every 32-element block its own scale, typically landing a 3-4x weight-size reduction versus fp16 with modest quality loss.

Compute Units: CPU, GPU, or the Neural Engine

compute_units is a hint to the scheduler, not a guarantee. CPU_ONLY and CPU_AND_GPU are hard constraints the runtime respects; ALL permits ANE scheduling but the actual placement is decided by Core ML at load time based on op support, dtype, and shape characteristics. The practical consequences show up in conversion behavior: the adjust_io_to_supported_types pass exists precisely because ANE-friendly models want fp16 boundaries, and the converter will warn when symbolic shapes or unsupported dtypes force fallbacks. If you have worked with ONNX or other interchange formats, the mental model is similar — a target-agnostic graph — except here the “target” is a family of Apple chips with a compiler stack you cannot inspect, so coremltools encodes a lot of hard-won knowledge about what the ANE actually accepts into passes and opset gating.

Honest Limits

The macOS/Xcode coupling is real. predict() runs only on macOS (10.13 minimum, 12.0+ for packages), the specification version you target must be supported by the installed Core ML framework, and new opsets (iOS17/iOS18) require new-enough OSes to load at all — you cannot ship an iOS18-spec model to an iOS15 device. Keeping a matrix of target OS versions and testing each exported package against the oldest one you support is not optional.

ANE coverage is a moving target. compute_units=ALL frequently produces a model that partially runs on the Neural Engine with the rest falling back to GPU or CPU, and the fallback decisions happen inside the closed-source runtime — coremltools cannot tell you exactly which subgraphs landed where. Op coverage in the torch frontend is similarly incomplete: any node kind without a registered handler raises NotImplementedError, and the frontend explicitly rejects dynamically quantized torch models, pointing you at the coremltools.optimize APIs instead (see the check around L136 of the torch ops.py transcription module). Complex control flow, exotic dtype tricks, and very new torch releases tend to need a wait-and-retry.

Quantization is not free. Int8/int4 and palettization reduce weight size substantially, but activation distributions that were fine in fp16 can degrade noticeably in int4, especially for small models or aggressive per_tensor granularity — the config surface exists precisely so you can trade granularity against size. Budget time for get_weights_metadata plus an eval harness, and consider keeping sensitive layers at higher precision. Finally, note what this stack is not: it is not a training runtime (that is MLX or PyTorch again), it is not cross-platform (for that world you would look at Executorch or plain ONNX tooling), and its Python-only predict path makes it a poor fit for server-side serving outside Apple hardware.
entry.summary: A source tour of apple/coremltools: the conversion flow from PyTorch and TensorFlow into Core ML, the MIL intermediate representation, graph passes, and post-training quantization.
